## E1. Question and hypothesis

**Question:** Are the years observed at five FLUXNET towers climatologically "normal" — i.e., how far do tower-year mean temperature and total precipitation deviate from the 1970–2000 WorldClim normals at the tower locations?

**Hypothesis:** Tower-years are on average **warmer** than the 1970–2000 normal (because the observation years 2000–2026 lie after the normal period, during which climate warmed), and the **driest** towers (low WorldClim BIO12) show the **largest relative precipitation anomalies**, because in dry climates a given absolute precipitation change translates into a larger relative anomaly and interannual variability is higher.

**Why these five towers are a reasonable test:** the set spans a wide climatic gradient — tropical savanna (AU-Dry, BIO1 ≈ 27 °C), alpine meadow (CN-HaM, BIO1 ≈ −0.7 °C), temperate sites (CA-Ca2, FR-Hes) and an irrigated Mediterranean-agricultural site (US-Bi1) — with annual precipitation from ~400 to ~1600 mm. That spread is what the second part of the hypothesis (dry towers → larger relative anomalies) needs. It is a small, non-random sample (n = 5 towers), so the test is descriptive rather than inferential.

## E3. Methods

**Download.** All scripts were provided with the course and run unchanged with `--student 18`, which selects my five towers (AU-Dry, CA-Ca2, CN-HaM, FR-Hes, US-Bi1) from `tower_sets_block4.csv`. `02_worldclim.py` downloads the WorldClim 2.1 5′ base rasters (bioclimatic variables plus monthly temperature and precipitation normals) and samples them at the tower coordinates. `04_soilgrids.py` reads the SoilGrids 2.0 Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFFs directly from the ISRIC server via per-property VRTs and samples the pixel under each tower. `09_merge.py` reads the FLUXNET daily (`DD`) files from the local snapshot zip. One problem surfaced during the analysis (not during download): the FLUXNET precipitation at CN-HaM is unusable — see below.

**Extraction.** WorldClim and SoilGrids are sampled at the single grid cell containing the tower coordinates (WGS 84 lat/lon; SoilGrids internally uses a custom equal-area CRS, handled by `pyproj` in the script). No window averaging was used — the assignment asks for the nearest cell, and the scale implications of that choice are discussed in E5.

**Processing.** FLUXNET daily values with the fill value −9999 are treated as missing. Years are kept only if they have ≥ 300 daily records (all years passed) and start in 2001 or later (4 FR-Hes years from 1997–2000 dropped, because they overlap the 1970–2000 normal period). Annual `TA_mean` is the mean of daily `TA_F`; annual `P_sum` the sum of daily `P_F`. WorldClim BIO1/BIO12 are used directly (°C, mm). SoilGrids values are converted from integer maps by the script's d-factor (clay/sand in %, averaged over the 0–5, 5–15 and 15–30 cm depths to a 0–30 cm value). The three tables are joined on `site_id`.

**Data-quality check on precipitation.** Before computing anomalies I checked whether `P_F` is measured or model-derived. **CN-HaM fails:** its `P_F` is identical to the ERA5-derived `P_ERA` on every day, `P_F_QC` is 0 everywhere (no measured contribution), and the resulting ~3 000 mm yr⁻¹ contradicts both the WorldClim normal (468 mm) and the published climate of the Haibei station on the north-eastern Tibetan Plateau (~500–600 mm yr⁻¹). The FLUXNET product's ERA5 precipitation for this site is broken, so CN-HaM is **excluded from the precipitation anomaly** (dP_pct = NA) but kept for the temperature anomaly (its `TA_F` is 95% measured and matches BIO1 well).

**Analysis.** For each tower-year *y* at tower *s*:

$$dT_{s,y} = TA_{s,y} - BIO1_s \qquad dP_{s,y} = 100 \cdot \frac{P_{s,y} - BIO12_s}{BIO12_s}$$

I report the mean dT, the fraction of tower-years warmer than normal, the fraction of tower-years drier than normal (over the 63 tower-years with usable precipitation), per-site means, and a descriptive correlation between mean dP_pct and SoilGrids clay/sand across the 4 towers with usable precipitation (n = 4 — descriptive only, no inference).

## E4. Results

Across **77 tower-years** (2001–2026, 5 towers), the mean temperature anomaly is **dT = +0.38 K**; **48 of 77 tower-years (62 %)** were warmer than the 1970–2000 normal. Of the **63 tower-years with usable precipitation** (CN-HaM excluded), **34 (54 %)** were drier than normal.

![Tower-year climate anomalies relative to the WorldClim 1970–2000 normals: temperature anomaly (K) vs. relative precipitation anomaly (%). Each point is one tower-year; colours are towers. CN-HaM has no precipitation anomaly (broken FLUXNET precipitation, see E3) and appears only on the temperature axis.](../outputs/figures/block5_fig1_anomaly_scatter.png)

Per-site means:

```{python}
#| echo: false
site_anom = df.groupby("site_id")[["dP_pct", "dT"]].mean()
site_anom.round(2)
```

The warming signal is dominated by **FR-Hes** (+1.34 K, 25 of 26 years warmer) and **AU-Dry** (+0.37 K, 13 of 17 warmer); **CA-Ca2** (−0.11 K), **CN-HaM** (−0.32 K) and **US-Bi1** (−0.68 K) are on average slightly cooler than normal. For precipitation, **CA-Ca2** is strongly drier than normal (−28 %, all 11 years), while **FR-Hes** is wetter (+15 %) and AU-Dry and US-Bi1 are near normal (−2 %).

Second angle — do dry towers show larger relative precipitation anomalies? Across the 4 towers with usable precipitation, mean dP_pct correlates **positively with clay content (r = +0.82)** and weakly negatively with sand (r = −0.23). This is the **opposite** direction of the hypothesis: the driest tower in the set (US-Bi1, BIO12 = 396 mm) has a near-normal anomaly, while the wettest (CA-Ca2, 1 596 mm) is the driest relative to normal.

## E5. Discussion

The hypothesis is **partially supported**. The warming part holds: tower-years are on average +0.38 K warmer than the 1970–2000 normals and 62 % of tower-years are warmer, which is what one expects given that the observation years (2001–2026) postdate the normal period. But it is carried almost entirely by FR-Hes and AU-Dry; the three other towers are slightly cooler than normal, so "warmer than normal" is not universal. The precipitation part is **not supported**: the driest tower does not have the largest relative anomaly, and the clay correlation goes the opposite way (r = +0.82). With n = 4 towers this correlation is descriptive anyway — one tower (CA-Ca2) largely determines it.

**Scale.** WorldClim cells are 5′ ≈ 9 km across — one to two orders of magnitude larger than a flux footprint (100 m–1 km). In complex terrain (CN-HaM on the Tibetan Plateau edge, CA-Ca2 in coastal British Columbia) the 9 km cell can differ substantially from the tower's local climate, so part of the "anomaly" may be a scale mismatch rather than real interannual variability. SoilGrids at 250 m is much better matched to the footprint scale, so the soil comparison is the more defensible one — though the 0–30 cm clay/sand values are still a static map compared against multi-year flux-tower precipitation, a weak physical link.

**Limitations.** (1) The CN-HaM precipitation in the FLUXNET product is broken (fully ERA5-derived, ~3 000 mm yr⁻¹ vs. ~500–600 mm published), which cost one of five towers for the precipitation analysis and shows how sensitive the anomaly computation is to product quality control. (2) Confounding site effects: CA-Ca2 is a clearcut stand (harvested 1999/2000) whose local microclimate differs from the grid normal, and US-Bi1 is irrigated alfalfa, so its tower precipitation anomaly does not reflect water stress. With more time I would add more towers per climate zone to make the clay/sand comparison meaningful, and replace the broken ERA5-derived precipitation with a station or gauge-based product.
